passage:
First week of term. Harsha from Rukmini's lab group said he'd lost his wallet and needed five hundred rupees for the lab manual. Rukmini handed it over without a second thought.
Two weeks later. He asked again, for bus fare home, and whether she could "just type up" his lab report because he was swamped. She did both, staying up past midnight.
The following Saturday. In the canteen she heard him tell someone he'd been to three films that week. Something in her chest went tight. On Monday she found him. "I'm happy to study with you. But I can't lend more until the first two are back, and your report is yours to write." Harsha looked annoyed, then shrugged. She walked away shaky, but lighter.

qa.q: What did Harsha say he needed five hundred rupees for?
qa.a: He said he needed it for the lab manual.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she heard about the three films?
qa.a: Her chest went tight; she felt hurt and began to suspect her kindness was being used.

qa.q: What limit did Rukmini set on Monday, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: She offered to study together but refused more loans until the first two were back and handed the report back to him, keeping her generosity without being used.

qa.q: What might Harsha's annoyed look show about how he saw Rukmini's help?
qa.a: It suggests he had come to expect her help as a given, so a limit surprised him.

grounding: Over a few weeks a trusting young woman lends and helps freely, notices she is being used, and sets a limit.

passage:
Disha, you remind me of me at twenty. Your Mama trusted everyone. In college, a friend named Anil needed help every week: my notes, my scooter, a little money "till Friday". Friday never came, but I kept saying yes, because saying no felt mean. Then one night he borrowed the scooter and returned it with an empty tank and a dent, and not a word. I sat on the steps and felt like a fool. My father said something I still use: "Kindness is yours to give, not theirs to take." After that I asked myself one question: does this person give anything back, even a thank you? I still help people, Disha. I just stopped handing my keys to everyone who asks.
Your Divyansh Mama

qa.q: What condition was the scooter in when Anil returned it?
qa.a: It came back with an empty tank and a dent.

qa.q: What did young Divyansh feel sitting on the steps that night?
qa.a: He felt like a fool, realising his trust had been used.

qa.q: What question did Divyansh start asking himself after that night?
qa.a: Whether the person gives anything back, even a thank you, which let him keep helping without being used.

qa.q: What might Divyansh's father have wanted him to understand with 'Kindness is yours to give, not theirs to take'?
qa.a: His father probably wanted him to see that kindness is a choice, not a debt others can collect, so he could keep helping without being used.

grounding: An uncle recalls how his trusting generosity was used at twenty and how he learned to spot it and set limits.

passage:
Thursday
Neelam asked for money again tonight. 'Just till Monday, Lakshmi, you're the only one who gets it.' That's what she said in August, and in September. I've never seen any of it back, and I've never asked, because asking felt rude. I also typed her lab records twice when she was 'sick', then saw her photos from the mall that same evening. I keep telling myself she's going through something. Maybe she is. But tonight I noticed she only knocks on my door when she needs something. I said I'd think about it. My stomach hurt all evening. I don't want to become someone who doesn't help. But I think I'm allowed to help in ways that don't empty me out. Tomorrow I'll call Akka and talk it through before I answer.
Lakshmi

qa.q: When had Neelam asked before, according to the diary?
qa.a: In August and in September.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling after saying 'I'll think about it'?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt uneasy and torn, stomach hurting, wanting to stay generous but noticing that Neelam only comes when she needs something.

qa.q: Is calling Akka before answering a wise step? Why?
qa.a: Yes; talking it over with someone trusted helps Lakshmi decide on a limit calmly, instead of giving in or drowning in guilt.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Lakshmi?
qa.a: Neelam seems to see Lakshmi as the one who always says yes, knocking only when she needs something.

grounding: Shows a young adult who assumes good intent and helps without limit, beginning to notice that her kindness is being used and to think about limits.

passage: In the kasba of Sehore, everyone knew Jyoti never said no. When her neighbour Sunaina came with cloth for 'my cousin's wedding, just two blouses, you're so quick', Jyoti stitched them at night after her own orders. Then two more, for another wedding. Then four. On Tuesday, at the weekly haat, Jyoti saw her own stitching, her neat double hem, on blouses hanging from Sunaina's stall with price tags. Her face went hot, then cold. She walked home slowly past the temple, thinking. She liked being the one who helped. She did not like being the one who was used. That evening Sunaina came with more cloth. Jyoti kept her hands on the sewing machine. 'I can't stitch these free any more. If you like, I'll teach you the hem on Sunday.' Sunaina's smile slipped. 'Oh. Okay.'

qa.q: Where did Jyoti see her own stitching?
qa.a: On blouses hanging from Sunaina's stall at the weekly haat, with price tags.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she saw the blouses at the stall?
qa.a: She felt shocked and used, her face going hot and then cold.

qa.q: Was offering to teach the hem a good limit? Why?
qa.a: Yes; it stops free work that was being sold, while still offering a fair, kind kind of help.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when her smile slipped?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably caught off guard and a little embarrassed, realising Jyoti had noticed.

grounding: Shows a generous young adult who assumes good intent, discovers her help is being exploited, and sets a limit.

passage:
Inside the kitchen cupboard of their shared flat in Lisbon, Noa kept a sticky note: Dalia – rent top-up, bus pass, concert ticket. She had never meant it as a bill; it was just so she wouldn't forget.
On Thursday Dalia leaned in the doorway. "Tiny favour? My card's being weird again. Could you cover the groceries? I'll pay you back Friday, promise."
Noa was already reaching for her wallet. Then she glanced at the note and noticed that every Friday on it had come and gone. The same week, Dalia had posted photos from a weekend away at the coast.
Noa's stomach tightened. She liked being the one people could count on. "I can't this time," she said, her voice wobbling. "And I'd like us to sit down and go through the list first."
Dalia rolled her eyes. "Seriously? I thought we were friends."
"We are. That's why I'm saying it."

qa.q: Where did Noa keep the sticky note?
qa.a: Inside the kitchen cupboard of their shared flat in Lisbon.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling when she said "I can't this time"?
qa.a: She felt anxious and torn: her stomach tightened and her voice wobbled, because she liked being someone people could count on but saw that every promised Friday had passed.

qa.q: What could Noa do next to protect both her kindness and herself?
qa.a: She could hold the talk about the list, stay friendly but firm, and if Dalia keeps asking, talk it through with someone she trusts before agreeing to help again.

qa.q: Why might Dalia react with an eye-roll?
qa.a: Dalia is used to Noa saying yes, so a no feels like a change in the friendship; being asked about the list may also embarrass her.

grounding: Shows a generous young adult noticing that her help is being taken for granted and starting to set a limit.
